clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis:
Answer: Sex differences were assessed using Welch's t-tests with effect sizes (Cohen's d). Regions showing significant sex differences (15 cortical regions, FDR-corrected) were further tested using ANCOVA including age of heaviest cannabis use onset and past-month cigarette smoking as covariates (partial η²). General linear models (GLMs) with sex interaction term tested associations between z-scores of sexually dimorphic regions and behavioral outcomes (MCQ craving, MJPS cannabis-associated problems, BIS impulsivity). Sensitivity analyses included age of heaviest use onset and past-month cigarette smoking. Significant associations: pars orbitalis z-score with MJPS (β=0.23, SE=0.11, p=0.043); superior parietal cortex z-score with MJPS (β=0.21, SE=0.08, p=0.014); precuneus z-score with MJPS (β=0.28, SE=0.10, p=0.004); postcentral gyrus z-score negatively with MCQ total (β=-0.11, SE=0.05, p=0.017).
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed:
Answer: Average z-scores across all regions were well within ±1.0 standard deviations of normative mean (z=0) for both males and females. No sex differences were observed in whole brain, total cerebral white matter, or total subcortical gray matter volume z-scores (all p's >0.05). However, a significant sex difference was observed in total cortical thickness (t(59)=3.01, p=0.004, Cohen's d=0.71), with males showing lower z-scores (M=-0.62, SD=1.47) than females (M=0.26, SD=0.97). Fifteen cortical regions, predominantly in frontal and parietal lobes, showed significant sex differences: 14 regions had greater cortical thickness z-scores in females (superior frontal gyrus, caudal middle frontal gyrus, pars opercularis, pars triangularis, pars orbitalis, precentral gyrus, paracentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus, banks of superior temporal sulcus, postcentral gyrus, supramarginal gyrus, superior parietal cortex, precuneus, cuneus), while medial orbitofrontal cortex showed greater z-scores in males. After ANCOVA controlling for age of heaviest use onset and past-month cigarette smoking, 9 regions maintained significance. Cerebellar gray matter z-scores showed sex differences (p=0.030) with greater z-scores in males, but this did not survive covariate adjustment. No sex difference was found in hippocampal z-scores (p=0.613). Three sexually dimorphic regions were associated with cannabis-related problems (MJPS): pars orbitalis (β=0.23, p=0.043), superior parietal cortex (β=0.21, p=0.014), and precuneus (β=0.28, p=0.004), with no sex interactions. Postcentral gyrus z-scores were negatively associated with cannabis craving (MCQ total: β=-0.11, p=0.017).
Confidence Rating: High

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes:
Answer: Findings of normative morphometric cortical thickness values argue against clinically significant cannabis-induced neurotoxicity/cortical atrophy. The sexually dimorphic effects may stem from sex-specific disruption of neurodevelopmental trajectories during adolescence (when participants initiated cannabis use). Previous literature shows that females who use cannabis have thicker frontal and parietal cortices relative to female controls, while males have thinner cortices relative to male controls. Results invoke hormonal influences on brain structure and the endocannabinoid system; gonadal hormones show bidirectional modulatory relationship with endocannabinoids which may be disrupted by chronic THC exposure. The association of greater cortical thickness with more cannabis-related problems suggests CUD-associated neurodevelopmental aberration may be especially detrimental to females, though associations were limited in number and effect size. Future longitudinal research is needed to determine clinical relevance and assess normative modeling in larger samples to examine outcomes in individuals with z-scores outside normal range.
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: The discussion section provides extensive interpretation of the clinical and scientific implications of the findings.
Supporting Text: Findings  of  normative  morphometric  cortical  thickness  values  in CUD argue against cannabis-induced neurotoxicity insofar as it could result  in  clinically  significant  cortical  atrophy... Our finding of a sexually dimorphic effect in CUD, though, is unique and may potentially  stem  from  sex-specific  disruption  of  neurodevelopmental trajectories of cortical development... results invoke the broader literature on hormonal influences on brain structure and the endocannabinoid  system... Our  findings  that  relate  greater  cortical thickness to more cannabis-related problems suggest that CUD-associated  neurodevelopmental  aberration  may  be  especially detrimental to females, but these associations were limited in number and  effect  size,  and  necessitate  replication

caa10_key_limitations.answer:
Answer: Modest sample size, particularly for females (n=22); reliance on retrospective self-report of cannabis use; restrictive inclusion/exclusion criteria may limit generalizability; secondary analysis of baseline RCT data without systematic control of factors affecting cortical thickness (hormonal contraceptive use, menstrual cycle phase, time of day for scans, long-term tobacco use history, physiological states, medical comorbidities); small female sample may not be representative of broader CUD population; cross-sectional design precludes causal inference about whether sex differences result from neurodevelopmental disruption by cannabis; sex assessed by self-report only rather than karyotype or hormone concentration; several individuals had z-scores outside normal range but sample too small to examine outcomes in this subgroup.
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: The limitations are comprehensively discussed in the final paragraph of the Discussion section.
Supporting Text: Nonetheless, limitations of this  work  include:  modest  sample  sizes,  although  our  sample  is  still nearly double most of those used in previous studies... reliance on retrospective reporting of cannabis  use;  and  restrictive  inclusion/exclusion  criteria  that  may impact the generalizability... factors that may influence cortical thickness such as hormonal  contraceptive use (Petersen et al., 2015; Pletzer et al., 2010), menstrual cycle phase (De Bondt et al., 2013; Pletzer et al., 2010), time of day when scans were conducted (Dieleman et al., 2017), tobacco use (Karama et al., 2015), or specific physiological states and medical comorbidities (Dieleman et al., 2017) were not systematically controlled... Most importantly, this work is a cross-sectional observational study; as such, our hypothesis that sex differences in cortical thickness are due to disruption of neurodevelopmental processes by cannabis use remains speculative. This study also only assessed sex via self-report, rather than by karyotype or hormone concentration.
Location: materials/Martin2025.pdf.md:235-236

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a single-site study using a Siemens 3T Prisma scanner at the Medical University of South Carolina. The study combined baseline data from two separate clinical trials (varenicline and TMS) for CUD. FreeSurfer v6.0 was used for segmentation, generating 1344 regional measures. NOMIS software (Python-based, available at https://github.com/medicslab/NOMIS) was used to compute normative z-scores. The NOMIS reference sample characteristics beyond n=6909 and age range 18-100 are not detailed in this paper; readers should refer to Potvin et al. (2016, 2017, 2022) for complete reference sample details. Supplementary materials include: Supplementary Table 1 showing correlations of cortical thickness z-scores across hemispheres (all regions showed significant bilateral correlations, r=0.311-0.866, all p<0.01), and Supplementary Table 2 showing hippocampal and cerebellar gray matter volume z-score correlations across hemispheres and sex differences. All segmentation was performed in subject space with no co-registration or normalization across subjects. Statistical analyses used R version 4.2.2. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure was used to control false discovery rate for multiple comparisons across cortical thickness regions. Participants abstained from cannabis and alcohol for 24 hours prior to scanning (confirmed via saliva sample). Study received IRB approval from MUSC and Stanford University (for TMS trial). Trial registration numbers: NCT02892110 (varenicline) and NCT03144232 (TMS). The study reports equal representation of males and females from each trial (χ² test, p=1.000).
